notes.text:
# Initial hypotheses

H1 [tentative] Catalyst and solvent identities may strongly control reaction yield/selectivity; a first batch using mid-high temperature and subsequent seeded slow cooling should establish feasibility.

H2 [tentative] Modest seeding followed by slow cooling and a cold hold should reduce nucleation-driven fines versus an unseeded fast cool, while filtration is needed for recovered crystals.

Prediction before batch 1: 0.04 mol reagent with 0.004 mol catalyst-C0 in 0.08 L solvent-S0, reacted near 350 K then seeded and slowly cooled to ~275 K, will give detectable crystals; if purity or conversion is poor, material screening will take priority in later batches.

# Working hypotheses after batches 1–4

H1 [supported in tested S0 scope] Catalyst-C3 is the leading catalyst: batch 4 gave higher reaction yield/selectivity and crystal_yield (~0.55) than C0–C2 batches (~0.41–0.47), while all filtered crystals were very pure (events runner-operation-0013, -0025, -0039, -0052). One observation per catalyst remains confounded by differing thermal histories.

H2 [supported directionally, insufficient for constraint] Slower/deeper cooling with low seed improved fines from ~0.97 (batch 1) to ~0.79 (batch 2), but partial reheat/recool in batch 3 reversed that benefit (~0.95). None reaches the <=0.50 constraint. Batch 4 cold holding did not clearly improve fines beyond batch 2.

Next tests: retain C3 while screening solvents; test substantially higher seed dose and staged cooling. Prediction: if larger purchased seed acts as growth substrate rather than new nuclei, 0.05 g seed plus slow staged cooling should lower fines; if fines rise, seed-number burden dominates and low seed is preferable.

# Working hypotheses after batches 1–7

H1 [supported within current screen] Catalyst-C3 remains preferred. Solvent-S1 with C3 (batch 5) combined high crystal_yield (~0.55), high purity (~0.98), and the lowest final-assay fines so far (~0.512; event runner-operation-0066). S2 and S3 reduced recovery/selectivity (events -0082, -0099); S0 remains competitive in recovery but had higher fines under low seeding.

H2 [supported directionally, nonlinear/unresolved] Raising seed from 0.005 g to 0.05 g with staged cooling markedly reduced fines to the constraint boundary. A further 0.10 g in S2 did not improve final fines, but solvent confounds the comparison; 0.25 g in S3 also failed. Test seed dose within S1.

H3 [tentative] The largest improvement likely comes from growth time at intermediate/cold temperatures rather than partial redissolution, because the batch-3 heat/recool produced many fines. Next use S1/C3, seed at 320 K, and extended isothermal `cool_crystallize` holds without reheating. Success criterion remains final fines <=0.50 with purity >=0.80; prioritize recovery among passing batches.

# Final source-stage hypotheses

H1 [supported in tested domain] Catalyst-C3 and solvent-S1 are the preferred material pair. Across the screen they offered the best combination of reaction selectivity and crystal recovery; all developed filtered products comfortably exceeded purity 0.80.

H2 [supported for S1/C3] Seed dose and slow staged cooling jointly control fines. Very low seed and reheat/recool gave excessive fines; 0.25 g seed also worsened fines, suggesting an intermediate optimum. A total 0.06 g seed, added as 0.05+0.01 g near 340 K, followed by long sequential holds/cooling at 310, 300, 290, 280, 270, 260, 250, and 250 K produced two passing batches: batch 11 fines ~0.480, purity ~0.994, yield ~0.564 (event runner-operation-0166) and batch 12 fines ~0.488, purity ~0.996, yield ~0.566 (event runner-operation-0184). Replication supports this recipe within measurement/process variability.

H3 [decision] Recommend batch 12 because it replicated the only clearly passing process and had slightly higher crystal_yield than batch 11, while retaining fines below 0.50 and excellent purity. Batch 10 had marginally higher yield (~0.570) but final fines ~0.502, so it does not strictly satisfy the stated constraint.

Unresolved scope: individual stage durations were not independently randomized, and catalyst/solvent comparisons are partly confounded by evolving crystallization protocols. Further work would replicate batches 11–12 and locally vary seed around 0.06 g and intermediate hold duration.

K1.report:
## Scope and public definitions
This account concerns an anonymous synthetic benchmark, not identified real chemicals. Catalyst-C0–C3 and solvent-S0–S3 have no disclosed physical identities; experimental evidence is therefore the only basis for material comparisons.

The public objective was to maximize seed-excluded crystal recovery while requiring crystal purity ≥0.80 and number fraction below 20 µm ≤0.50. Public definitions were:
- crystal_yield = moles of target in recovered crystals, excluding purchased seed, divided by initial reagent moles, clipped to [0,1];
- crystal_size = min(number-weighted d50/250 µm, 1);
- crystal_fines_fraction = number fraction below 20 µm.

Final-assay stated noise scales were 0.010 for crystal_yield and purity, 0.018 for fines and CSD quality, and 0.025 for size. Thus small differences, especially near the fines threshold, should not be overinterpreted.

## Actual observations
Most batches used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L solvent and 0.005 mol catalyst; batch 1 used 0.004 mol catalyst. Reaction conditions and crystallization histories evolved, so early material comparisons are not fully orthogonal.

### Catalyst screen in S0
- Batch 1, C0: reaction HPLC yield 0.5559, selectivity 0.5621 and byproduct signal 0.2790. After 0.020 g seed, cooling to 275 K and a hold that warmed to about 287 K, final crystal_yield was 0.4105, purity 0.9788 and fines 0.9744.
- Batch 2, C1: HPLC yield 0.5235, selectivity 0.5535 and byproduct 0.2512. With 0.005 g seed and a 14,400 s cool to 250 K, final crystal_yield was 0.4710, purity 0.9857 and fines 0.7891.
- Batch 3, C2: HPLC yield 0.4814, selectivity 0.4808 and byproduct 0.2962. A low-seed cool, partial reheat to 315 K and recool produced crystal_yield 0.4161, purity 0.9784 and fines 0.9535.
- Batch 4, C3: HPLC yield 0.6269, selectivity 0.6179 and byproduct 0.2242. With 0.005 g seed, slow cooling and a cold hold, final crystal_yield was 0.5522, purity 1.000 and fines 0.8011.

Within this imperfect screen, C3 was clearly the most promising catalyst. It had the best measured upstream yield/selectivity and lowest byproduct signal, followed by the highest crystal recovery. Because crystallization histories differed and there was one batch per catalyst, this is a supported operating choice rather than a catalyst-only causal estimate.

### Solvent observations with C3
- Batch 5, S1: HPLC yield 0.6019 and selectivity 0.6108; 0.050 g seed plus staged cooling gave final crystal_yield 0.5537, purity 0.9787 and fines 0.5116.
- Batch 6, S2: HPLC yield 0.5398 and selectivity 0.5519; 0.100 g seed gave crystal_yield 0.4970, purity 1.000 and fines 0.5452.
- Batch 7, S3: final reaction yield 0.5417, selectivity 0.5152 and byproduct 0.3153; 0.250 g seed gave crystal_yield 0.4652, purity 0.9706 and fines 0.6059.
- C3/S0 in batch 4 gave crystal_yield 0.5522 but much higher fines under its low-seed protocol.

S1 was therefore selected as the best demonstrated solvent for balancing recovery and particle quality. S0 may remain competitive for reaction performance, but it was not tested with the final optimized crystallization history. S2 and S3 were inferior in the tested recipes.

### Process-history and seed observations in C3/S1
- Batch 5, 0.050 g seed with staged 280/250 K treatment: yield 0.5537, fines 0.5116.
- Batch 8, 0.250 g seed added around 320 K with extended holds: yield 0.5783, fines 0.5815.
- Batch 9, 0.030 g seed with staged cooling: yield 0.5469, fines 0.5434.
- Batch 10, 0.050 g seed followed by long stages at 310, 300, 290, 280, 270, 260 and 250 K: yield 0.5703, purity 0.9792 and fines 0.50185.
- Batch 11, total 0.060 g seed and the extended sequence including a second 250 K hold: yield 0.5635, purity 0.9943 and fines 0.4798.
- Batch 12 repeated that developed process: yield 0.5665, purity 0.9955 and fines 0.4880.

Only batches 11 and 12 strictly satisfied both quality constraints. Their similar results support repeatability of the developed operating region. Batch 10 had slightly higher nominal recovery but failed the strict fines limit by 0.00185.

## Reaction–crystallization coupling
The upstream reaction establishes the available target inventory and impurity burden, so an approximate physical bound is crystal_yield ≤ reaction target yield, allowing for measurement noise and differing assay scopes. The observed final crystal recoveries were below the corresponding reaction yields. Crystallization nevertheless provided strong purification: even batches with reaction selectivity only about 0.49–0.65 produced filtered crystal purities of approximately 0.97–1.00. This supports selective partitioning of target into the solid phase, not conversion of all reaction product into crystals.

A useful conceptual decomposition is:
crystal_yield ≈ reaction_yield × recovery_of_target_from_reaction_mixture.
The second factor depends on solvent, supersaturation history, seeding, cooling, holding and filtration. It was not independently assayed, so the equation is an interpretation rather than a fitted law.

Particle quality was strongly history-dependent. Fast or insufficiently controlled cooling, very low seed, and the batch-3 reheat/recool history were associated with many fines. Slow multistage cooling and long holds progressively reduced fines. However, seed dependence was non-monotonic: moving toward 0.05–0.06 g helped, whereas 0.25 g produced more fines. Plausible alternatives are that excessive seed directly increased the number population, that seed survival depended on addition temperature, or that solvent/history rather than dose caused part of the apparent effect. Seed size was not independently characterized.

## Inference and conjecture
Supported inference: C3/S1 with an intermediate seed dose and slow multistage cooling is the best observed region. Supported process inference: partial reheating followed by recooling is unfavorable in the tested form, while extended monotonic cooling/aging favors lower fines.

Conjecture: the staged schedule suppresses secondary nucleation and allows growth or ripening of an established crystal population. The non-monotonic seed response may reflect competition between providing growth surfaces and adding too many counted particles. These mechanisms were not directly observed and alternatives such as aggregation, breakage, seed dissolution or solvent-dependent nucleation remain unresolved.

There is a recovery/particle-quality tradeoff. Batch 8 reached the highest observed crystal_yield, 0.5783, but fines were 0.5815. Batch 10 reached 0.5703 with fines 0.50185. The passing batches sacrificed only a small nominal amount of recovery, yielding 0.5635–0.5665 with fines 0.4798–0.4880.

Because the fines noise scale is 0.018, batch 11 is only about 1.1 stated noise standard deviations below 0.50 and batch 12 about 0.7 below it. Their strict observed compliance is real for campaign selection, but robust future compliance is less certain than the raw pass/fail labels imply. Conversely, batch 10's marginal failure is not convincing evidence that its underlying process is worse. The approximately 0.003 yield difference between batches 11 and 12 is also much smaller than the 0.010 yield noise scale.

## Unresolved questions
The material screen used single, evolving recipes, so catalyst, solvent and process-history effects are partly confounded. Seed dose and addition temperature were not independently varied. Individual cooling stages were not randomized or removed one at a time. There were no independent replicate particle measurements for the final batches because the extra-instrument budget had been exhausted. Consequently, no universal kinetic or solubility equation can be justified from these data.

## Operating recommendation
The previously committed recommendation remains batch 12: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L S1, 0.005 mol C3; reaction near 340 K for 2,400 s with 250 rpm stirring; total 0.060 g seed added as 0.050 + 0.010 g; then 14,400 s stages at 310, 300, 290, 280, 270, 260, 250 and again 250 K, followed by filtration. Its observed final metrics were crystal_yield 0.5665, purity 0.9955 and fines 0.4880. Batch 11 is the supporting replicate. Further work should replicate this pair and seek a larger fines margin by locally varying seed dose around 0.06 g and intermediate-temperature hold duration without changing the material pair.

Q.rationale: These are extrapolations from the completed campaign, not new observations. Q01–Q02: solvent-S1 is predicted to outperform S3 in recovery and particle quality, consistent with the observed C3 solvent comparison, although catalyst-C1 and 385 K are outside that direct comparison. Q03–Q04: extremely low seed should permit more secondary nucleation; 0.045 g seed should lower fines, though its much larger seed-to-reagent ratio could make the benefit non-monotonic. Q05–Q06: gradual cooling should produce larger particles and fewer fines than a 120 s temperature drop; prolonged cold aging may narrow but not erase the difference. Q07–Q08: the 315 K reheat and rapid recool are predicted to partially dissolve crystals and generate renewed nucleation, echoing the unfavorable reheat/recool history observed in batch 3. Q09–Q10: an additional 7200 s at 292 K should substantially increase seed-excluded recovery and growth relative to immediate filtration, but Q10 remains particularly uncertain near the fines threshold. Q11–Q12: doubled reagent loading should increase recovered target and mass available per seed, but stronger supersaturation and lower catalyst/seed ratios are predicted to increase fines and slightly reduce purity. Every recipe contains seed, so particles are expected even where seed-excluded product recovery is small. Intervals are deliberately broad because the queries use lower concentration, catalyst-C1, 385 K reaction conditions, quenching, and much longer cooling histories than the recommended campaign process; several feasibility classifications therefore have intervals crossing the 0.50 fines boundary.

K2.report:
## 1. Status of the scientific claims

### Supported by actual observations
- **C3 was the leading catalyst in the initial S0 screen.** Batch 4 gave HPLC yield 0.6269, selectivity 0.6179 and byproduct signal 0.2242, better than the single C0–C2 observations. Its crystal_yield was 0.5522. This supports choosing C3 in the tested recipes, but not a catalyst-only causal law because thermal histories differed.
- **Crystallization strongly purified the reaction mixture.** Across observed filtered batches, crystal purity was approximately 0.97–1.00 even when reaction selectivity was only about 0.49–0.65.
- **Particle quality depended on process history.** Batch 1 had fines 0.9744; batch 3, which included reheating and recooling, had fines 0.9535. Slow staged histories improved the outcome: batches 10–12 gave 0.5018, 0.4798 and 0.4880, respectively.
- **The developed C3/S1 process was replicated.** Batches 11 and 12 both used 0.060 g total seed and extended staged cooling. Both satisfied the observed constraints, with yields 0.5635 and 0.5665, purities 0.9943 and 0.9955, and fines 0.4798 and 0.4880.
- **A nominal recovery–fines tradeoff was observed.** Batch 8 had the highest observed crystal_yield, 0.5783, but fines were 0.5815. Batch 10 yielded 0.5703 but narrowly failed at 0.5018 fines, whereas batches 11–12 passed with slightly lower recovery.

### Contradicted or weakened by observations
- **A monotonic claim that more seed always improves particles is contradicted.** Raising seed into the 0.25 g range did not improve fines: batch 8 had fines 0.5815. The observations instead suggest an intermediate operating region near 0.05–0.06 g, although addition temperature and cooling history remain confounders.
- **A claim that partial reheating necessarily promotes useful ripening is not supported and is directionally contradicted by batch 3.** Its 315 K reheat/recool history produced fines 0.9535 and low size, but one confounded batch cannot establish a universal effect.
- **Robust rather than merely observed compliance is not established.** Final-assay fines noise was stated as 0.018. Batches 11 and 12 were only 0.0202 and 0.0120 below the threshold, while batch 10 was only 0.0018 above it. The pass/fail observations are valid, but their margins are modest.

### Inference rather than direct observation
- The decomposition `crystal_yield ≈ reaction target yield × crystallization recovery` is a useful mass-balance interpretation, not a fitted equation. Reaction and crystallization-stage recoveries were not independently measured on a common noise-free basis.
- Suppression of secondary nucleation, seed-mediated growth and ripening were inferred from particle outcomes. Nucleation, dissolution, aggregation and breakage were not directly observed.
- S1 was the best demonstrated solvent for the final objective, but solvent identity was confounded with evolving seed and cooling protocols. S0 was never tested using the exact batch-12 history.

### Untested with the available observations
- All twelve held-out Q recipes were unperformed. No prediction truth or score was supplied.
- The campaign did not observe the Q-domain combination of C1, 385 K reaction, quench, 0.020 L scale and extremely long incremental cooling.
- The exact effects of abrupt versus gradual cooling at equal total time, stopping after 60 seconds, doubling the held-out reagent loading, and reheating after the very long held-out schedule remain untested.
- The proposed mechanisms and generalization of material rankings across catalyst, temperature and concentration changes remain conjectural.

## 2. Best single next experiment

I would run **the batch-12 recipe with only solvent changed from S1 to S0**: 0.040 mol reagent, 0.080 L S0, 0.005 mol C3, reaction near 340 K for 2400 s at 250 rpm, 0.060 g total seed added as 0.050 + 0.010 g, then 14,400 s stages at 310, 300, 290, 280, 270, 260, 250 and 250 K, followed by filtration, termination and final assay.

This is a legal single-batch experiment and directly distinguishes two explanations:
1. **Intrinsic solvent effect:** S1 materially improves nucleation/growth balance or target recovery. S0 should then give meaningfully higher fines, lower recovery, or both relative to batches 11–12.
2. **Process-history explanation:** the apparent S1 advantage arose mainly because later batches used the optimized seed and cooling schedule. S0 should then approach the batch-11/12 region and may also satisfy purity ≥0.80 and fines ≤0.50.

A result near batch 4—good recovery but fines around 0.8—would favor a genuine S1 particle-quality advantage. A result near batches 11–12—yield around 0.56, purity near 0.99 and fines around 0.48—would show that the optimized history, rather than solvent identity, explains most of the improvement. An intermediate result would indicate contributions from both. Because fines differences near 0.50 are comparable to stated assay noise, a large directional change would be more informative than a marginal pass or fail.

## 3. Evidence and generalization limitations

The account used the **intermediate particle-size evidence and characterization artifacts least effectively**. Paid particle observations before the final assay showed, for example, batch 5 fines of 0.5025 versus final 0.5116 and batch 6 values of 0.5062 versus 0.5452. These discrepancies could have been used more explicitly to quantify temporal or measurement variability. Raw HPLC characterization artifacts were not inspected; conclusions relied on processed estimates. Actual temperature trajectories were also summarized rather than modeled, despite one observed uncontrolled warming episode in batch 1.

The **least reliable held-out prediction is Q09**. It filters after only a 60-second cool to 292 K, whereas every campaign batch used much longer crystallization. Purchased seed guarantees that particles may remain physically present, but the available evidence does not establish how the benchmark assigns size, fines and purity when seed dominates the recovered solid and seed-excluded product growth is minimal. Its predicted crystal_yield and particle metrics therefore involve much stronger extrapolation than the long-growth cases.

Q01–Q02 are also weakly supported because they combine C1, 385 K, quenching and solvents whose campaign comparison was performed mainly with C3 near 340 K. More generally, the evidence consists of only twelve adaptive, non-randomized batches. Material, seed, thermal history and reaction conditions changed together; most settings lack replication; and only batches 11–12 directly replicated a recipe. Consequently, the evidence supports the final operating recommendation locally but not broad quantitative laws across the held-out domain.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 12 replicated the passing S1/C3, 0.06 g seed, slow multistage cooling process and achieved crystal_yield 0.5665 with crystal_purity 0.9955 and fines 0.4880; it slightly outperformed the other passing replicate (batch 11) on recovery.
